name: Hydrogen
summary: The lightest and most abundant element in the universe, forming stars and water.

name: Helium
summary: The second most abundant element in the universe; the only element that does not solidify at atmospheric pressure.

name: Lithium
summary: The lightest solid metal, widely used in rechargeable batteries and psychiatric medication.

name: Beryllium
summary: A stiff, lightweight metal toxic to humans; valued in aerospace and nuclear applications.

name: Boron
summary: A metalloid essential to plant growth; used in borosilicate glass and semiconductors.

name: Carbon
summary: The basis of all known life; exists as graphite, diamond, fullerene, and graphene allotropes.

name: Nitrogen
summary: Makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere and is essential to amino acids and nucleic acids.

name: Oxygen
summary: The third most abundant element in the universe; drives combustion and cellular respiration.

name: Fluorine
summary: The most electronegative and reactive element; used in Teflon and dental fluoride treatments.

name: Neon
summary: An inert noble gas famous for its brilliant red-orange glow in discharge tubes and signs.

name: Sodium
summary: A soft, highly reactive metal critical to nerve function and found in table salt.

name: Magnesium
summary: A lightweight structural metal; central atom of chlorophyll and essential for over 300 enzyme reactions.

name: Aluminium
summary: The most abundant metal in Earth's crust; prized for its light weight and corrosion resistance.

name: Silicon
summary: The second most abundant element in Earth's crust; foundation of modern semiconductor electronics.

name: Phosphorus
summary: Essential to DNA, RNA, and ATP; the first element discovered in modern history by a single individual.

name: Sulfur
summary: A bright yellow solid known since antiquity; used in fertilisers, gunpowder, and rubber vulcanisation.

name: Chlorine
summary: A toxic yellow-green gas used for water purification and PVC production.

name: Argon
summary: The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere; widely used as an inert shielding gas in welding.

name: Potassium
summary: A soft silvery metal vital to nerve impulses and muscle contraction; the symbol K comes from the Latin kalium.

name: Calcium
summary: The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust; essential for bones, teeth, and cellular signalling.

name: Scandium
summary: A light transition metal used in high-strength aluminium–scandium alloys and solid-oxide fuel cells.

name: Titanium
summary: A strong, lightweight, corrosion-resistant metal central to aerospace, medical implants, and white pigment.

name: Vanadium
summary: A hard silvery-grey metal that strengthens steel alloys; essential trace element in some organisms.

name: Chromium
summary: Gives stainless steel its corrosion resistance and rubies their red colour; has a half-filled d-shell anomaly.

name: Manganese
summary: An essential trace element and key alloying agent in steel; the most common nodule metal on ocean floors.

name: Iron
summary: The most used of all metals; defines the Iron Age and is the primary constituent of Earth's core.

name: Cobalt
summary: A ferromagnetic metal used in lithium-ion battery cathodes, jet-engine superalloys, and blue pigments.

name: Nickel
summary: A corrosion-resistant metal critical to stainless steel, electric vehicle batteries, and coinage.

name: Copper
summary: Humanity's first worked metal; indispensable for electrical wiring due to its outstanding conductivity.

name: Zinc
summary: Used in galvanising steel to prevent rust and essential to hundreds of human enzymes.

name: Gallium
summary: One of few metals that melts near room temperature; crucial for GaN semiconductors and LEDs.

name: Germanium
summary: Predicted by Mendeleev as eka-silicon; used in fibre optics, infrared optics, and early transistors.

name: Arsenic
summary: A toxic metalloid historically used as poison; now used in semiconductors and wood preservatives.

name: Selenium
summary: A photoconductive nonmetal used in solar cells, photocopiers, and as an essential dietary trace element.

name: Bromine
summary: One of only two liquid elements at room temperature; used in flame retardants and water treatment.

name: Krypton
summary: A noble gas used in high-performance photographic flash lamps and certain laser systems.

name: Rubidium
summary: A highly reactive alkali metal used in atomic clocks and quantum computing experiments.

name: Strontium
summary: Gives fireworks their brilliant crimson colour; radioactive Sr-90 is a major fission product.

name: Yttrium
summary: A soft metal used in superconductors, phosphors for TV screens, and yttrium-aluminium-garnet lasers.

name: Zirconium
summary: A corrosion-resistant metal used for nuclear reactor fuel rod cladding due to its low neutron-capture cross-section.

name: Niobium
summary: A superconductor at low temperatures and a key microalloying element in high-strength low-alloy steel.

name: Molybdenum
summary: One of the highest-melting metals; an essential enzyme cofactor for nitrogen fixation in plants.

name: Technetium
summary: The lightest element with no stable isotopes; Tc-99m is the world's most widely used medical radioisotope.

name: Ruthenium
summary: A rare platinum-group metal used as a hardener in platinum alloys and in electrodes for chlorine production.

name: Rhodium
summary: One of the rarest and most valuable metals; the primary catalyst in automotive three-way catalytic converters.

name: Palladium
summary: Absorbs up to 900 times its volume of hydrogen; key catalyst in catalytic converters and hydrogen purification.

name: Silver
summary: The element with the highest electrical and thermal conductivity; prized for jewellery, currency, and photography.

name: Cadmium
summary: A toxic heavy metal used in nickel–cadmium batteries and as a neutron absorber in nuclear reactors.

name: Indium
summary: A soft metal essential for indium-tin oxide (ITO) coatings on touchscreens and flat-panel displays.

name: Tin
summary: One of the first metals smelted; essential to bronze-age civilisation and still used in solder.

name: Antimony
summary: A brittle metalloid used in flame retardants, lead-acid battery plates, and semiconductors.

name: Tellurium
summary: A rare metalloid used in phase-change memory devices, thermoelectrics, and cadmium-telluride solar cells.

name: Iodine
summary: A violet-black solid essential for thyroid hormones; the heaviest stable halogen.

name: Xenon
summary: A dense noble gas used in high-intensity arc lamps, ion propulsion engines, and anaesthesia.

name: Caesium
summary: The most electropositive stable element; Cs-133 defines the SI second via atomic clock transitions.

name: Barium
summary: Used in barium sulfate as a radiocontrast agent for gastrointestinal X-ray imaging.

name: Lanthanum
summary: The first lanthanide; used in hybrid vehicle batteries, camera lenses, and hydrogen storage.

name: Cerium
summary: The most abundant rare-earth element; used in catalytic converters, glass polishing, and flint igniters.

name: Praseodymium
summary: A rare-earth metal used in high-strength permanent magnets, protective goggles for welders, and jet engines.

name: Neodymium
summary: Forms the world's strongest permanent magnets (Nd2Fe14B), enabling electric motors, hard drives, and headphones.

name: Promethium
discovered_by: Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, Charles Coryell
summary: The only lanthanide with no stable isotopes; used in nuclear-powered miniature batteries and luminous paint.

name: Samarium
summary: Forms samarium–cobalt magnets that retain strength at very high temperatures; Sm-153 is used in cancer therapy.

name: Europium
summary: The most reactive rare-earth element; its red and blue phosphors give CRT monitors their colour.

name: Gadolinium
summary: Has the highest neutron-absorption cross-section of all elements; Gd chelates are MRI contrast agents.

name: Terbium
summary: Produces green phosphorescence in trichromatic fluorescent lamps and solid-state drives.

name: Dysprosium
summary: Added to neodymium magnets to maintain coercivity at elevated temperatures in electric vehicles.

name: Holmium
summary: Has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element; used in powerful magnet pole pieces.

name: Erbium
summary: Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) are the backbone of global telecommunications networks.

name: Thulium
summary: The rarest naturally occurring lanthanide; Tm-170 is used in portable X-ray machines.

name: Ytterbium
summary: A fully filled f-shell lanthanide used in optical fibre amplifiers and atomic clock research.

name: Lutetium
summary: The last and densest lanthanide; Lu-177 is a targeted radiotherapy agent for certain cancers.

name: Hafnium
summary: Used in nuclear reactor control rods and high-κ gate dielectrics in modern transistors.

name: Tantalum
summary: Extremely corrosion-resistant; used in miniature capacitors for mobile phones and surgical implants.

name: Tungsten
summary: Has the highest melting point of all elements; used in incandescent filaments, cutting tools, and armour-piercing ammunition.

name: Rhenium
discovered_by: Ida Noddack, Walter Noddack, Otto Berg
summary: One of the last naturally occurring elements discovered; critical in superalloys for jet engine turbine blades.

name: Osmium
summary: The densest naturally occurring element; used in hard-wearing alloys for pen tips and electrical contacts.

name: Iridium
summary: The most corrosion-resistant metal; the Cretaceous–Paleogene iridium anomaly evidences the asteroid impact.

name: Platinum
summary: A dense noble metal used in catalytic converters, jewellery, and as the former standard kilogram.

name: Gold
summary: The most malleable metal and humanity's premier store of value; relativistic effects give it its yellow colour.

name: Mercury
summary: The only metal liquid at room temperature; relativistic electron contraction explains its unusual phase.

name: Thallium
summary: A highly toxic post-transition metal once used in rat poison; now used in medical imaging (Tl-201).

name: Lead
summary: One of the oldest metals known; a dense, soft metal used in radiation shielding and lead-acid batteries.

name: Bismuth
summary: The heaviest stable element; used in low-melting alloys, cosmetics, and as a non-toxic replacement for lead.

name: Polonium
summary: A highly radioactive element discovered by Marie Curie and named after her homeland Poland.

name: Astatine
discovered_by: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie, Emilio Segrè
summary: The rarest naturally occurring element; At-211 is investigated for targeted alpha-particle cancer therapy.

name: Radon
summary: A naturally occurring radioactive noble gas that seeps from uranium-containing rocks into buildings.

name: Francium
summary: The second rarest naturally occurring element and the least electronegative of all elements.

name: Radium
summary: The heaviest alkaline earth metal; historically used in luminous watch dials and cancer treatment.

name: Actinium
summary: The first actinide; Ac-225 is a promising alpha-emitter for targeted radiotherapy.

name: Thorium
summary: A fertile nuclear fuel material; molten-salt thorium reactors are a promising low-waste nuclear energy path.

name: Protactinium
summary: A rare, highly radioactive actinide; Pa-231 is used in oceanic sediment dating.

name: Uranium
summary: The heaviest naturally occurring element; powers nuclear reactors via fission of U-235.

name: Neptunium
summary: The first transuranic element; produced in nuclear reactors as a byproduct of uranium irradiation.

name: Plutonium
summary: A fissile material used in nuclear weapons and reactor fuel; Pu-238 powers deep-space probes.

name: Americium
summary: Found in every household smoke detector; Am-241 ionises air to detect combustion particles.

name: Curium
summary: Named after Pierre and Marie Curie; Cm-244 alpha sources power space-mission instruments.

name: Berkelium
summary: A highly radioactive synthetic element produced in microgram quantities in nuclear reactors.

name: Californium
summary: Cf-252 is a neutron source used to start nuclear reactors and in portable neutron-activation analysis.

name: Einsteinium
summary: Discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test; only nanogram amounts have ever been isolated.

name: Fermium
summary: Also discovered in Ivy Mike bomb debris; the heaviest actinide producible in nuclear reactors in observable amounts.

name: Mendelevium
summary: Named after Dmitri Mendeleev; the first element produced one-atom-at-a-time using ion bombardment.

name: Nobelium
summary: Named after Alfred Nobel; shows unusual +2 oxidation state stability due to its full f-shell.

name: Lawrencium
summary: The last actinide; named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.

name: Rutherfordium
discovered_by: Albert Ghiorso et al., Dubna team
summary: The first transactinide element; named after Ernest Rutherford and confirmed to behave like hafnium.

name: Dubnium
discovered_by: Dubna team, Albert Ghiorso et al.
summary: Named after Dubna, Russia; a synthetic transactinide element studied only via single-atom chemistry.

name: Seaborgium
summary: Named after Glenn Seaborg, the first element named after a living person; behaves like tungsten.

name: Bohrium
discovered_by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
summary: Named after Niels Bohr; synthesised in quantities of a few atoms per experiment.

name: Hassium
discovered_by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
summary: Named after Hesse, Germany; predicted to be the densest element; OsO4-like tetroxide confirmed.

name: Meitnerium
discovered_by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
summary: Named after Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of nuclear fission; no chemistry has been performed.

name: Darmstadtium
summary: Named after Darmstadt, Germany; a transactinide element predicted to share properties with platinum.

name: Roentgenium
summary: Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays; predicted to be a noble-metal-like element.

name: Copernicium
discovered_by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg et al.
summary: Named after Nicolaus Copernicus; relativistic effects are predicted to make it a gas at room temperature.

name: Nihonium
summary: The first element discovered in Asia; named after Nihon (Japan); confirmed in 2016 by IUPAC.

name: Flerovium
summary: Named after Flerov Laboratory; relativistic effects may give it noble-gas-like volatility despite being in group 14.

name: Moscovium
summary: Named after Moscow Oblast; synthesised by bombarding americium-243 with calcium-48 ions.

name: Livermorium
summary: Named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory; the heaviest confirmed group-16 element.

name: Tennessine
summary: Named after Tennessee; the second-heaviest known element and the heaviest halogen group member.

name: Oganesson
summary: The heaviest confirmed element; despite being a noble gas by position, relativistic effects predict it is a solid at room temperature.
